title: Scaling writes: bursts, queues and load shedding
seriesDescription: How to scale write-heavy systems in an interview: vertical scaling and database choice, sharding and partition keys, vertical partitioning, queues and load shedding, batching, hierarchical aggregation, and the resharding and hot-key deep dives.
description: Why autoscaling is not a panacea, how queues absorb bursts, when they mask a deeper problem, and how to shed low-value writes.
source: Study notes: the scaling writes pattern

questions.prompt: Why is autoscaling not a complete answer to a 4x peak?

options.text: Scaling takes time and, for databases, can mean downtime or reduced throughput while it happens.
options.why: Right: slow exactly when you need it.

options.text: Autoscaling is illegal in production in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Not a real constraint.

options.text: Autoscaling only works for read traffic without any extra configuration.
options.why: It can scale write capacity too.

options.text: Autoscaling makes writes free during peaks.
options.why: It does not remove cost or delay.

questions.explanation: Without help, you would have to run at 25% utilisation to handle a 4x burst.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of putting a queue in front of the database?

options.text: Burst absorption: the queue buffers spikes while the database writes at a steady rate.
options.why: Right: it decouples accepting from processing.

options.text: It makes the database faster per write for most everyday workloads.
options.why: It does not speed the database.

options.text: It makes writes synchronous and immediately visible.
options.why: It makes them asynchronous.

options.text: It removes the need for a database in a typical production setup.
options.why: The data still must be stored.

questions.explanation: Clients may need a way to check later that the write completed.

questions.prompt: When is a queue the wrong tool?

options.text: When steady-state input exceeds database capacity, so the backlog grows without bound.
options.why: Right: it only hides the problem.

options.text: When bursts are short-lived and the system can tolerate delay in a typical production setup.
options.why: That is when queues shine.

options.text: When you want to absorb a flash of traffic for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: A good use; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: When processing can be retried safely.
options.why: Retries are easier with a queue.

questions.explanation: Use queues for short bursts, not to patch a database that cannot handle the steady load.

questions.prompt: True or false: with a write queue, the app server only knows the write was queued, not that it reached the database.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the confirmation is only that it was accepted.

options.text: False
options.why: It does not confirm the database write.

questions.explanation: Clients often need a callback or status check, and reads may briefly miss the new data.

questions.prompt: What should you check before adding a queue?

options.text: Whether the product tolerates delayed writes and inconsistent reads.
options.why: Right: a queue can break key requirements.

options.text: Whether the queue vendor has a nice logo.
options.why: Not a technical criterion.

options.text: Whether the database is already at zero load.
options.why: Not the point; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Whether every write is financially critical, because queues need that.
options.why: It is the opposite concern.

questions.explanation: Ask about tolerance for delay at the requirements stage.

questions.prompt: During overload, which writes should a location-tracking system drop first?

options.text: Updates within seconds of a previous one, since a fresher update is coming anyway.
options.why: Right: they are the least valuable.

options.text: The first location ever sent by a new user without any extra configuration.
options.why: It is high value; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Every write from every user equally at random as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Prioritise rather than drop blindly.

options.text: Payments, to protect location data.
options.why: Business-critical writes come first.

questions.explanation: For analytics, drop impressions before clicks.

questions.prompt: Why is load shedding better than letting everything fail?

options.text: It keeps a bad situation (too much load) from turning into a disaster (system failure).
options.why: Right: a release valve.

options.text: It guarantees no user is affected.
options.why: Some users are affected.

options.text: It lets the system accept unlimited traffic in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: It limits what is accepted.

options.text: It removes the need for capacity planning under normal operating conditions as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: You still plan capacity.

questions.explanation: Decide in advance which writes matter most to the business.

questions.prompt: Clients send fresh GPS points every few seconds and traffic spikes. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Shed the redundant updates, since a newer one will replace them.
options.why: Right: a queue would only build a stale backlog.

options.text: Queue everything, however large the backlog becomes in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Stale data would be processed late.

options.text: Autoscale the database and accept downtime without any extra configuration.
options.why: That is slow and risky.

options.text: Stop all location updates for every user.
options.why: That removes the feature entirely.

questions.explanation: When data is superseded quickly, dropping is better than buffering.
